Your friendship matters, but Priya is not part of your circle, and you should not make a spectacle of someone who has said something makes her uncomfortable. The tradition may feel personal, and your friends may see it as one more reason not to trust you. That hurt could make you lose their trust for a while, so approach the conversation carefully: thank them for the time they spent on the project and explain that this joke goes beyond what she can hear without being upset. Even if the tradition is tied to shared memories, it does not have to be worth mocking someone whose pain it causes.

I would suggest removing the slide rather than weakening your objection simply because your friends expect you to go along. A tradition can be meaningful to you and your friends, but using someone else’s embarrassment or humiliation for amusement crosses a line when you know exactly why they dislike it. Priya is not part of your group, so this is not just a small inside joke among your friends; it is being shared in front of many people who may not understand its history. If your objection seems petty, you can phrase it as avoiding a slide that could cause hurt even if others find it funny. Your friends may feel disappointed, especially if the slideshow was already mostly finalized, but respect for another person’s discomfort matters more.

It is reasonable that your grade has shared inside jokes, but a photo of someone being humiliated should not become part of the class’s public record if they do not want it there. You can suggest a less personal slide, such as a funny caption or a general memory of senior year. Your friends may feel disappointed because this was something they were counting on, and that is understandable. Still, the person whose image is being used deserves more than a polite shrug.

It does not need to accuse anyone of ill intent; it can describe what was said, how it sounded, and what happened afterward. That kind of joke can be embarrassing for someone who has just joined a school community, and it deserves a calm reminder that everyone belongs here. Linh can write it without naming individuals or using angry language. Some of her friends may be disappointed that she is reporting on them, but the report should reflect that every student’s comfort matters.

I would recommend giving Mateo a reduced penalty rather than the full zero and referral, while explaining why. He used someone else’s work under pressure, and a zero will be painful, especially at his moment of instability. A lower score, a note in the gradebook, a conversation about sources, and a written warning may reflect the seriousness of the mistake without making him feel permanently defined by it. Mr. Okonkwo should connect him with tutoring or a school social worker so he does not continue to fall behind. This recommendation comes at the cost of a strong example to other students, and it is not an excuse. But a student who is already vulnerable deserves help, not another reason to feel alone.

Recommend that Mr. Okonkwo reduce the consequence or defer judgment for now. A student who is struggling with housing should not lose a grade and a disciplinary referral on top of a difficult situation at home. The teacher can require Mateo to write a reflection on the policy, keep him enrolled until school services can be accessed, and monitor whether the behavior recurs. This response does not excuse academic dishonesty, but it recognizes that a child in unstable housing may act out in ways a teacher can help before labeling him permanently. The school should not pretend his needs do not exist because his mistake happened inside class.

Recommend that Mr. Okonkwo keep the academic penalty private but give Mateo an alternative opportunity to demonstrate learning. A zero and formal referral may expose him to further disruption and embarrassment at home. He did not take the easy route, since he owned up immediately rather than pretending he wrote the paragraphs himself. But the immediate problem now is that he cannot get back into school without help. Mr. Okonkwo can let Mateo make it up through extra work, a tutoring session, or another low-stakes assignment, explain it as a personal emergency rather than a rule violation, and tell him clearly that repeating that behavior would be taken seriously.

Recommend giving Mateo a modified penalty instead of the referral and zero: partial credit for content, a warning, and extra help preparing for the next test. His home situation matters; sleeplessness and disorientation may have made him act out of anxiety rather than indifference. A clean record would protect him from a permanent mark while still holding him accountable for the work he failed to do. This will not erase the problem or forgive the copying fully. It does make the consequence fit the moment better, with space for a teacher to support a student who is struggling rather than punishing him for panic.
